rv.q: Rightfully so, because 'Dancin'' is as metal as musical theater gets.
This is a show hell-bent on making sure that you have fun, laughs, good times at any cost.
Here is something it surely can never touch, thank the memories of 1978, thank God, thank Fosse.
The show is a joy every time it puts down its ax.

The show is essentially a jukebox musical built around Fosse's choreographic legacy, but it lacks the narrative drive or thematic coherence that might give it more lasting impact beyond the undeniable pleasure of watching skilled dancers execute Fosse's inimitable moves.
The show is a showcase for some excellent dancers, but it feels more like a museum piece than a living, breathing work of theater.
“Unhappily, the first revival of Fosse’s all-dance, plotless revue ... does not represent the man at his most inspired...
Bob Fosse's Dancin' doesn't just make old moves fresh — it makes us feel like we're discovering Fosse anew.
Cilento sought to update the show and introduce Bob Fosse to a new generation — and he mostly succeeds.
Dancin’, a celebration of everything Fosse, is a love letter to the makers and performers, and clearly pitched to the people who appreciate the artistry in every pointed toe and crescent jump.
If you want to see some of the best triple-threats in the biz, head on over to experience some true Fosse magic.
Dancin' is mostly spectacular, until it suddenly isn't—before ramping itself up again for the finale.
There’s a smug irony to this presentation of Americana that’s especially unwarranted.
What might she have thought of this dubious enterprise?
This new incarnation feels like an advanced class in Fosse in which all the students have learned how the pronounce well enough for us to understand but they still have a heavy accent.
What you're about to see is nothing like the scenery-less version of A Doll's House over at the Hudson Theatre.
Cilento’s exceptional reimagining manifests how Fosse stylized the art form toward an apotheosis of vibrance, sexiness, rigor and grace.
For anyone looking to tap their toes and clap their jazz hands at a Broadway show, Bob Fosse's Dancin' delivers.
Others may want to shuffle off to another this season’s many new Broadway offerings.

cn.t: Critics find this Fosse revival thrilling to watch but lacking substance, praising the exceptional dancers and high-energy choreography while noting the show feels more like a glitzy showcase than a cohesive theatrical experience.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.
